We study space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory (including interacting theories) on static space-times. We first consider Euclidean quantum field theory on a static Riemannian manifold, and show that the isometry group is generated by one-parameter subgroups which have either self-adjoint or unitary quantizations. We analytically continue the self-adjoint semigroups to one-parameter unitary groups, and thus construct a unitary representation of the isometry group of the associated Lorentzian manifold. The method is illustrated for the example of hyperbolic space, whose Lorentzian continuation is Anti-de Sitter space.

Its central aim is to understand how symmetries present in a Euclidean formulation of the theory can be related to the corresponding symmetries of a Lorentzian space-time after analytic continuation.

The analysis begins with Euclidean quantum field theory formulated on a static Riemannian manifold. In this setting, the geometry admits a distinguished time direction, and the quantum theory can be studied using Euclidean methods. The Euclidean framework is especially useful because it provides a rigorous setting for constructing quantum fields and analyzing their covariance properties under the isometries of the underlying manifold.

This distinction is important because it determines how each Euclidean symmetry behaves under analytic continuation to Lorentzian signature.

The self-adjoint semigroups obtained in the Euclidean theory are then analytically continued. Through this continuation, they become one-parameter unitary groups. In this way, the Euclidean symmetry data are used to construct a unitary representation of the isometry group of the associated Lorentzian space-time. This provides a systematic bridge between Euclidean quantum field theory on a static Riemannian manifold and the corresponding Lorentzian quantum field theory, preserving the relevant space-time symmetries at the quantum level.

The method is illustrated through the example of hyperbolic space. In the Euclidean setting, hyperbolic space serves as the Riemannian manifold on which the quantum field theory is defined. The text develops a framework for understanding space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory on static space-times. The central idea is to begin not directly with a Lorentzian quantum field theory, but with a Euclidean quantum field theory formulated on a static Riemannian manifold. In this Euclidean setting, the geometry possesses isometries whose infinitesimal generators give rise to semigroups of transformations on the quantum Hilbert space. These semigroups encode the action of Euclidean symmetries at the level of the quantized theory.

A key point of the analysis is that, under suitable assumptions, these quantized semigroups admit analytic continuation. This continuation transforms the Euclidean symmetry structure into the corresponding Lorentzian one. In particular, the analytically continued operators become unitary, thereby producing a unitary representation of the isometry group of the associated static Lorentzian manifold. This provides a rigorous mechanism by which space-time symmetries in the Lorentzian quantum field theory can be recovered from the Euclidean theory.

The construction is especially important because static space-times naturally allow a relation between Riemannian and Lorentzian geometries through a Wick rotation of the time coordinate. In the Euclidean theory, time evolution is typically represented by contraction semigroups, while in the Lorentzian theory it should be represented by unitary groups. The analytic continuation procedure bridges these two descriptions: Euclidean time translations become Lorentzian time translations, and more generally, Euclidean isometries give rise to Lorentzian space-time symmetries.

The text illustrates this method with the example of hyperbolic space and Anti-de Sitter space. Hyperbolic space serves as the Euclidean static Riemannian manifold, while Anti-de Sitter space appears as the corresponding Lorentzian manifold obtained by analytic continuation. The isometry group acting on hyperbolic space is continued to the isometry group of Anti-de Sitter space, and the quantized semigroup representation associated with the Euclidean theory becomes a unitary representation in the Lorentzian theory. This example demonstrates concretely how the Euclidean approach can be used to construct and analyze quantum field theories with nontrivial space-time symmetries.

Overall, the text shows that Euclidean quantum field theory on static Riemannian manifolds provides a powerful route to Lorentzian quantum field theory on static space-times. By studying the analytic continuation of quantized isometry-generated semigroups, one obtains a systematic construction of unitary representations of Lorentzian isometry groups. This connects Euclidean methods, reflection positivity, and the representation theory of space-time symmetry groups, offering a mathematically coherent way to recover physical symmetries after Wick rotation.
outputs.L5:
Euclidean, Riemannian, and Lorentzian geometries are three important frameworks for understanding space, distance, and structure.

**Euclidean geometry** is the familiar geometry of flat space. It is based on the principles developed by the ancient Greek mathematician Euclid and describes ordinary shapes such as lines, circles, triangles, and planes. In Euclidean space, the shortest distance between two points is a straight line, parallel lines never meet, and the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. This geometry is widely used in everyday measurements, engineering, architecture, and classical physics.

**Riemannian geometry** generalizes Euclidean geometry to curved spaces. Instead of assuming that space is flat, Riemannian geometry allows the distance between points and the angles between directions to vary from place to place. A surface such as a sphere is a simple example: the shortest paths are not straight lines in the Euclidean sense, but curved paths called geodesics. On a sphere, for instance, great circles play the role of “straight lines.” Riemannian geometry is fundamental in modern mathematics and has applications in fields such as topology, differential geometry, data analysis, and general relativity.

**Lorentzian geometry** is closely related to Riemannian geometry but is designed to describe spacetime rather than purely spatial distances. In Lorentzian geometry, the metric has a different signature, allowing a distinction between space-like, time-like, and light-like directions. This structure is essential in Einstein’s theory of special and general relativity, where gravity is understood as the curvature of spacetime. Unlike Euclidean or Riemannian geometry, Lorentzian geometry incorporates time as a central dimension and explains how events are connected by causal relationships.

Together, these geometries show how the concept of distance can be adapted to different settings. Euclidean geometry describes flat space, Riemannian geometry describes curved spaces, and Lorentzian geometry describes the geometry of spacetime. Each plays a crucial role in mathematics, physics, and our understanding of the universe.

counterfactuals.output:
We present a framework for the quantization of isometry groups in Euclidean quantum field theory on static Riemannian manifolds and for their analytic continuation to Lorentzian space-times. Let \((M,g_E)\) be a complete static Riemannian manifold admitting a distinguished Euclidean time function and a group \(G\) of isometries preserving the geometric and spectral data of a Euclidean field theory. Starting from a reflection-positive Schwinger functional or, equivalently, a Euclidean measure satisfying covariance under \(G\), we construct the physical Hilbert space by Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction. The subgroup preserving the time-reflection structure acts by unitary operators on the reconstructed Hilbert space, while Euclidean time translations give rise, after reflection positivity, to a self-adjoint Hamiltonian bounded from below.

We then analyze the infinitesimal action of the Euclidean isometry algebra on correlation functions and determine conditions under which its generators admit closable representatives on the physical Hilbert space. For static backgrounds of the form
\[
(M,g_E)=(\mathbb{R}\times \Sigma,\, d\tau^2+h),
\]
with \((\Sigma,h)\) a Riemannian Cauchy manifold, analytic continuation in the Euclidean time variable \(\tau\mapsto it\) yields the Lorentzian metric
\[
g_L=-dt^2+h,
\]
and transforms the Euclidean semigroup generated by the time-translation operator into the Lorentzian unitary evolution group. Under suitable analyticity, reflection positivity, and covariance assumptions, the continued \(n\)-point Schwinger functions define Wightman distributions on the associated static space-time, satisfying positivity, locality, covariance, and the spectral condition relative to the static Hamiltonian.

The resulting Lorentzian symmetry representation is obtained by analytic continuation of the Euclidean isometry representation. Compact spatial isometries quantize directly as unitary symmetries, while Euclidean transformations mixing time and space continue to the corresponding Lorentzian boosts or dynamical symmetries when the complexified isometry algebra admits compatible real forms. This identifies a precise correspondence between Euclidean geometric invariance and Lorentzian quantum symmetry: the quantized Euclidean isometry group acts initially on Schwinger data, descends through reflection positivity to the physical Hilbert space, and analytically continues to a unitary representation of the Lorentzian isometry group whenever the underlying static geometry and correlation functions possess the required holomorphic extension properties.

This construction clarifies the role of static Riemannian geometry in Euclidean quantum field theory, establishes a rigorous mechanism for passing from Euclidean covariance to Lorentzian covariance, and provides a natural setting for studying quantum fields on curved static backgrounds, including ultrastatic space-times, thermal field theories, and symmetric manifolds admitting nontrivial analytic continuations.

Starting from a Euclidean theory satisfying reflection positivity with respect to a distinguished time reflection, we apply the Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction procedure to obtain a Hilbert space, a self-adjoint Hamiltonian, and unitary time evolution after analytic continuation to Lorentzian signature.
